code.title: Middleware chain and URL resolution in a request
code.python:
# Mini model of Django's request life: middleware -> URL resolver -> view -> back out
def make_mw(name):
    def factory(get_response):          # called once, gets the next layer
        def mw(request):
            request["log"].append(name + " in")      # before the view
            response = get_response(request)
            request["log"].append(name + " out")     # after the view
            return response
        return mw
    return factory

def detail(request, pk):
    return "article %d" % pk

URLS = [("articles/", int, detail)]     # (prefix, converter, view)

def resolve_and_call(request):
    path = request["path"]
    for prefix, conv, view in URLS:      # first full match wins
        if path.startswith(prefix):
            return view(request, conv(path[len(prefix):]))  # converter: "7" -> 7
    return "404"

handler = resolve_and_call
for name in reversed(["Security", "Session", "Auth"]):  # first listed = outermost
    handler = make_mw(name)(handler)

req = {"path": "articles/7", "log": []}
print("request:", req["path"])
print("response:", handler(req))
print("order:", " > ".join(req["log"]))

followUps:
Add it in a small middleware near the top of MIDDLEWARE, so every other layer and the view can see it. It reads the incoming X-Request-ID header (or makes a UUID), stores it on request.request_id, calls get_response, then copies it onto the response header.

rid = request.headers.get("X-Request-ID") or uuid4().hex
request.request_id = rid
response = get_response(request)
response["X-Request-ID"] = rid

Putting it first means even responses made by short-circuiting middleware carry the id. Cost is O(1) per request.

include() lets a URL pattern hand the rest of the path to another URL list. The resolver matches the prefix, strips it, and tries the nested patterns on what is left.

Example: path("shop/", include(shop_urls)) and a nested path("item/<int:pk>/", ...). For shop/item/7/ the prefix shop/ matches, then item/7/ is tried against the nested list, giving pk=7. Captured values from both levels are merged, and an optional namespace is added for reverse(). Patterns are tried in order, so the first full match wins.

code.title: FBV vs CBV: as_view makes a fresh instance

followUps:
Because LoginRequiredMixin must run its check before the real view logic, and Python looks up methods left to right through the MRO. Listed first, its dispatch() runs first and redirects anonymous users before anything else.

class Page(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView): ...   # correct
class Bad(ListView, LoginRequiredMixin): ...    # ListView.dispatch wins

In the wrong order the generic view's dispatch is found first, so the login check is skipped and anonymous users get the page, a silent security hole.

as_view() returns an ordinary function (the view closure) that Django can put in a URL pattern. On each request that function creates a new instance of your class, sets request, args and kwargs on it, and calls dispatch().

So state kept on self lives for one request only. Class attributes, in contrast, are shared by all requests and threads, so never mutate them (for example a list on the class). Creating the instance costs almost nothing.

code.title: Lazy QuerySet with result cache

followUps:
Because if qs: loads every row into memory just to answer yes or no, while exists() asks the database for a single row.

With 1,000,000 matching rows, if qs: fetches and builds a million objects (O(N) time and memory), and exists() runs roughly SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1, which is fast with an index. The one case where if qs: is fine is when you will iterate the same QuerySet next, because the cache is reused and you pay for one query instead of two.

Print str(qs.query) to see the SQL text, or use qs.explain() to see the database plan. Without running anything you can inspect it in the shell.

print(qs.query)
from django.db import connection
print(connection.queries)   # needs DEBUG=True

The django.db.backends logger at DEBUG level prints every executed statement with parameters. Note that str(qs.query) shows parameters inlined in a way that may not be exactly what is sent to the database.

code.title: N+1 vs select_related vs prefetch_related query counts
code.python:
# N+1 vs JOIN vs "IN" prefetch, counting the SQL statements with sqlite3
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE author(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE book(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, author_id INTEGER);
INSERT INTO author VALUES (1,'Ann'),(2,'Bo'),(3,'Cy');
INSERT INTO book VALUES (1,'A1',1),(2,'A2',1),(3,'B1',2),(4,'C1',3);
""")
count = [0]
db.set_trace_callback(lambda sql: count.__setitem__(0, count[0] + 1))

def run(label, fn):
    count[0] = 0
    result = fn()
    print("%-16s queries=%d %s" % (label, count[0], result))

def n_plus_one():                      # 1 query + one per book
    out = []
    for bid, title, aid in db.execute("SELECT * FROM book").fetchall():
        name = db.execute("SELECT name FROM author WHERE id=?", (aid,)).fetchone()[0]
        out.append((title, name))
    return out

def select_related():                  # one JOIN query
    return db.execute("SELECT b.title, a.name FROM book b JOIN author a ON a.id=b.author_id").fetchall()

def prefetch_related():                # 2 queries, stitched in Python
    books = db.execute("SELECT * FROM book").fetchall()
    ids = sorted({b[2] for b in books})
    marks = ",".join("?" * len(ids))
    names = dict(db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM author WHERE id IN (%s)" % marks, ids))
    return [(b[1], names[b[2]]) for b in books]

for label, fn in [("N+1", n_plus_one), ("select_related", select_related), ("prefetch_related", prefetch_related)]:
    run(label, fn)

followUps:
When the JOIN produces many duplicated or very wide rows. A JOIN repeats the parent columns on every child row, so large text columns get copied again and again.

Example: 100 authors each with a 50 KB bio and 20 books each: select_related style JOIN on a multi-valued relation would send 2,000 rows each carrying the bio (about 100 MB), while prefetch_related sends 100 bios once plus 2,000 small book rows. select_related also cannot follow many-valued relations, and a JOIN over many tables can make the optimizer choose a bad plan.

Make the queryset prefetch or join the data in get_queryset() and have the method field only read what is already loaded. Never run a query per object inside get_serializer_method.

qs = Order.objects.select_related("customer").prefetch_related("items")
# in the serializer
def get_total(self, obj):
    return sum(i.price for i in obj.items.all())  # uses cache

Use .all() in Python, not .filter(), since .filter() ignores the prefetch cache. Guard it with assertNumQueries.

code.title: F expressions and NOT with NULLs
code.python:
# F expressions (DB-side arithmetic) and Q NULL behaviour, shown with sqlite3
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE item(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, stock INT, rating INT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO item VALUES (?,?,?)", [(1, 5, 5), (2, 5, 2), (3, 5, None)])

# Python read-modify-write: two "requests" read the same value -> lost update
a = db.execute("SELECT stock FROM item WHERE id=1").fetchone()[0]
b = db.execute("SELECT stock FROM item WHERE id=1").fetchone()[0]
db.execute("UPDATE item SET stock=? WHERE id=1", (a - 1,))
db.execute("UPDATE item SET stock=? WHERE id=1", (b - 1,))
print("lost update, stock =", db.execute("SELECT stock FROM item WHERE id=1").fetchone()[0])

# F("stock") - 1  ->  SET stock = stock - 1, computed inside the database
db.execute("UPDATE item SET stock=5 WHERE id=1")
db.execute("UPDATE item SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id=1")
db.execute("UPDATE item SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id=1")
print("F update, stock    =", db.execute("SELECT stock FROM item WHERE id=1").fetchone()[0])

# ~Q(rating__lt=4): Django adds IS NOT NULL so NULL ratings are matched by the NOT
naive = db.execute("SELECT id FROM item WHERE NOT (rating < 4)").fetchall()
django = db.execute("SELECT id FROM item WHERE NOT (rating < 4 AND rating IS NOT NULL)").fetchall()
print("naive NOT  ids:", [r[0] for r in naive])
print("Django ~Q  ids:", [r[0] for r in django])

followUps:
Use one atomic database-side update with F, so concurrent requests cannot overwrite each other: Post.objects.filter(pk=pk).update(likes=F("likes") + 1).

This becomes SET likes = likes + 1, a single statement the database locks the row for, so 100 simultaneous likes give exactly +100. The Python version (p.likes += 1; p.save()) reads 5 twice and writes 6 twice, losing a like. Cost is one query, O(1). For per-user uniqueness add a unique (user, post) row and count rows instead.

They differ for multi-valued relations: one call means "one related row has both", two calls mean "no row has a, and no row has b".

For plain columns on the same row, exclude(a=1, b=2) removes rows where a=1 AND b=2 (NOT (a=1 AND b=2)), but exclude(a=1).exclude(b=2) removes rows where a=1 OR b=2. Row (a=1, b=5): the first keeps it, the second drops it. Chaining is the stricter filter.

code.title: atomic, savepoints and on_commit
code.python:
# atomic, savepoints and on_commit, modelled on sqlite3 (manual transaction control)
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)   # we issue BEGIN/COMMIT ourselves
db.execute("CREATE TABLE t(v TEXT)")
callbacks = []

class atomic:
    depth = 0
    def __enter__(self):
        self.name = "sp%d" % atomic.depth
        db.execute("BEGIN" if atomic.depth == 0 else "SAVEPOINT " + self.name)
        atomic.depth += 1
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        atomic.depth -= 1
        outer = atomic.depth == 0
        if exc_type:
            db.execute("ROLLBACK" if outer else "ROLLBACK TO " + self.name)
            if outer: callbacks.clear()          # on_commit callbacks are discarded
        else:
            db.execute("COMMIT" if outer else "RELEASE " + self.name)
            if outer:
                for fn in callbacks: fn()        # run only after the outermost commit
                callbacks.clear()
        return False

with atomic():
    db.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES ('outer')")
    callbacks.append(lambda: print("on_commit: send email"))
    try:
        with atomic():                           # inner block = savepoint
            db.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES ('inner')")
            raise ValueError("boom")
    except ValueError:
        print("inner rolled back, outer continues")
print("rows:", [r[0] for r in db.execute("SELECT v FROM t")])

followUps:
Because after an IntegrityError the database marks the whole transaction as broken (PostgreSQL: "current transaction is aborted"), and further queries fail with TransactionManagementError.

Wrap the risky statement in its own inner atomic() and catch the error outside it, so only a savepoint is rolled back.

try:
    with transaction.atomic():
        Item.objects.create(sku=s)
except IntegrityError:
    ...   # outer transaction still usable

Use TestCase.captureOnCommitCallbacks(execute=True), because TestCase wraps each test in a transaction that never commits, so callbacks would not run otherwise.

with self.captureOnCommitCallbacks(execute=True) as cbs:
    make_order()
self.assertEqual(len(cbs), 1)
self.assertEqual(len(mail.outbox), 1)

Alternatively use TransactionTestCase, which really commits but is slower because it flushes tables after each test.

code.title: Migration plan as a dependency graph

followUps:
A squashed migration replaces a long run of old migrations with one equivalent migration, so a fresh database applies one step instead of, say, 80.

It lists the migrations it replaces; databases that already applied them keep working, and new ones use the squash. Create it with squashmigrations app 0001 0080, deploy it everywhere, then delete the old files and drop the replaces line. It saves startup time for test databases and keeps the graph small.

Because inside RunPython you must use the models as they were at that migration, not today's code. apps.get_model("shop", "Order") returns a historical model matching the schema at that point.

If you import the real model, it may have fields that do not exist yet (the query fails) or later-added methods that behave differently, so the migration breaks months later on a fresh database. The historical model has no custom methods, only fields, so copy any needed logic into the migration.

code.title: Building the middleware chain in reverse

followUps:
Because the authentication middleware reads the session to find the logged-in user. SessionMiddleware loads request.session from the cookie, and AuthenticationMiddleware then sets request.user using that session.

Reversed, request.session would not exist yet when the user is looked up, and Django's system check (admin.E410) complains. Order is outermost-first: the session is attached on the way in and saved to the cookie on the way out.

Under ASGI Django adapts middleware so it can be sync or async. Each middleware declares sync_capable and async_capable, and Django wraps calls to match, which costs a thread hop for each mismatch.

Write async middleware with async def __call__ and mark it with markcoroutinefunction, or use @sync_and_async_middleware. If one layer is sync-only, Django runs it in a thread pool, so a single sync layer can slow every request. Avoid blocking calls in async layers.

code.title: Signals run synchronously and bulk paths skip them
code.python:
# A tiny signal dispatcher: receivers run synchronously, and bulk paths skip them
class Signal:
    def __init__(self):
        self.receivers = {}
    def connect(self, fn, dispatch_uid=None):
        self.receivers[dispatch_uid or id(fn)] = fn    # dispatch_uid blocks duplicates
    def send(self, **kw):
        for fn in self.receivers.values():
            fn(**kw)                                   # same thread, same transaction

post_save = Signal()
profiles = []

def create_profile(instance, created):
    if created:
        profiles.append("profile for " + instance)

post_save.connect(create_profile, dispatch_uid="make_profile")
post_save.connect(create_profile, dispatch_uid="make_profile")   # ignored: same uid

users = []
def save(name):                       # like Model.save(): fires post_save
    users.append(name)
    post_save.send(instance=name, created=True)

def bulk_create(names):               # like bulk_create(): no signals
    users.extend(names)

save("ann")
bulk_create(["bo", "cy"])
print("users   :", users)
print("profiles:", profiles)
print("missing profiles for:", [u for u in users if "profile for " + u not in profiles])

followUps:
Connect them in AppConfig.ready(), because it runs once after all apps are loaded, so models can be imported safely.

class ShopConfig(AppConfig):
    def ready(self):
        from . import signals  # noqa

Put @receiver functions in signals.py and import it there. Importing in models.py can cause circular imports, and connecting inside a view reconnects on every call. Use dispatch_uid to guard against double registration.

Test the effect, not the wiring: call the real code (User.objects.create(...)) and assert the result (the profile exists). To test a receiver alone, call it directly with fake arguments.

If the receiver does something slow, patch the side effect (mock.patch("app.signals.send_mail")). If it uses on_commit, use captureOnCommitCallbacks(execute=True). To prove a receiver is connected, check post_save.has_listeners(User). Remember bulk_create in a test will not trigger it.

code.title: Serializer validation order

followUps:
Override validate_<field> for a single field's rule and create() or update() for the writing, because DRF does not write nested data by itself.

Pop the nested data out of validated_data, save the parent, then save the children, all inside transaction.atomic().

items = validated_data.pop("items")
order = Order.objects.create(**validated_data)
Item.objects.bulk_create(
    [Item(order=order, **i) for i in items])

For updates you must decide whether missing children are deleted, kept or matched by id.

Because it exposes every model field, including ones you add later, such as is_staff or password, which can leak data or let clients write fields they should not.

List fields explicitly: fields = ("id", "name", "email"). A new column then changes the API only when you choose, and reviewers can see the contract. It also lets you mark read_only_fields deliberately, avoiding mass-assignment problems.

code.title: Permissions, 401 vs 403

followUps:
Check the owner for writes and allow safe methods for everyone, in has_object_permission.

class IsOwnerOrReadOnly(BasePermission):
    def has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj):
        if request.method in SAFE_METHODS:
            return True
        return obj.owner == request.user

It runs only through get_object(), so detail routes are covered, but list views must filter with get_queryset(). Pair it with IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly.

Enforce it in the queryset, so every query is already limited to the caller's tenant, and add a permission as a second guard.

def get_queryset(self):
    return Invoice.objects.filter(tenant=self.request.user.tenant)

Filtering at the base makes list, detail, update and delete all safe, and other tenants' objects return 404 rather than 403, which leaks nothing. Put it in a shared base viewset or custom manager, and write tests that log in as tenant A and request tenant B's ids.

code.title: Offset vs keyset pagination
code.python:
# Offset vs keyset (cursor) pagination on sqlite3, with a row inserted between pages
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE post(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, created INT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO post VALUES (?,?)", [(i, i) for i in range(1, 9)])  # newest = highest

def offset_page(n, size):
    return [r[0] for r in db.execute(
        "SELECT id FROM post ORDER BY created DESC, id DESC LIMIT ? OFFSET ?", (size, n * size))]

def keyset_page(cursor, size):
    c, i = cursor if cursor else (10**9, 10**9)
    rows = db.execute(                      # fetch size+1 to learn if a next page exists
        "SELECT id, created FROM post WHERE (created, id) < (?, ?) "
        "ORDER BY created DESC, id DESC LIMIT ?", (c, i, size + 1)).fetchall()
    page, has_next = rows[:size], len(rows) > size
    return [r[0] for r in page], (page[-1][1], page[-1][0]) if has_next else None

p0 = offset_page(0, 3)
cur_ids, cursor = keyset_page(None, 3)
print("page 1 offset:", p0, "keyset:", cur_ids)
db.execute("INSERT INTO post VALUES (9, 9)")           # new post arrives
print("page 2 offset:", offset_page(1, 3), "<- repeats 6")
print("page 2 keyset:", keyset_page(cursor, 3)[0], "<- no repeat")

followUps:
It fetches one extra row. Ask for page_size + 1 rows; if you get the extra one back, a next page exists, and you drop it before returning.

With size 20, request 21: getting 21 means "more", getting 17 means "last page". DRF's CursorPagination does exactly this, so it issues no COUNT(*). This costs O(log n + page) with an index instead of a full-table count.

Use a stable sort order made of the relevance score plus the id as a tie-breaker, and put both in the cursor. Page-number pagination is also acceptable if you only show a few top pages.

Scores can change between requests, so results may shift; for a consistent session, snapshot the ranked id list (or keep a search "point in time") and page through it. Search engines such as Elasticsearch offer search_after with sort values for exactly this. Deep offsets are expensive, so cap the depth, for example 10,000 results.

Use FastAPI-style streaming: return a StreamingHttpResponse from an async view that yields chunks as the model produces them, served under ASGI.

async def chat(request):
    async def gen():
        async for tok in llm_stream(prompt):
            yield f"data: {tok}\n\n"
    return StreamingHttpResponse(gen(),
        content_type="text/event-stream")

Run under Uvicorn or Daphne, not plain WSGI, and avoid middleware that buffers the body. The browser reads it as server-sent events.

Migrate when the framework's cost is bigger than its benefit for that service, for example when most work is waiting on many outside APIs and you need thousands of concurrent connections.

Move to FastAPI when the admin, ORM and auth are barely used, or the service is a thin typed wrapper. Move back to Django when you keep rebuilding auth, migrations, admin and permissions by hand. Do it by service, behind the same API, not as a big rewrite, and measure first (latency, concurrency, team speed).
